newsitem.title: USA: FCC takes step to salvage wireless phone companies.
newsitem.headline: FCC takes step to salvage wireless phone companies.

text.p: Regulators are taking the first step in what could become a major effort to salvage cash-strapped companies struggling to pay the government more than $10 billion for wireless phone licenses.
The Federal Communications Commission announced late Monday it will formally consider making it easier for dozens of small companies to pay for airwave licenses sold at two recent FCC auctions.

Congress and the White House are counting on the proceeds to reduce the deficit. But financial problems plaguing several top bidders have raised doubts over whether the more than $10 billion will all be collected.
Pocket Communications Inc., the No. 2 bidder at last year's high-flying wireless phone auction, has filed for bankruptcy protection after bidding $1.4 billion for 43 licenses.
Others -- including top bidder NextWave Telecom Inc., with winning bids of $4.7 billion -- have asked the FCC for help.
"This is the first step to re-evalulate whe whole ball of wax and determine what should be done," an FCC official said.

The agency's wireless bureau said it will seek public comment on ways to restructure the payment terms for the licenses to offer a new generation of cellular phone service known as "personal communications services," or PCS.
A Wall Street executive predicted the move would likely amount to "a fairly sizeable restructuring of the payments."

The bids have become loans from the government, with the auction winners paying interest on the money due. The auction that ended last year raised $10.2 billion. Only small companies were allowed to bid under special financial terms.
The other auction concluded in January and raised $2.5 billion for the government. The small companies whose plight is under scrutiny accounted for a portion of that amount.
Among the range of options floated or under study:
-- Allow the companies to default on their payments and then reauction the licenses.
-- Handle each company on a case-by-case basis. That way, payments could be restructured to meet individual needs.

-- Defer interest payments for several years, such as five, to give companies time to build their PCS networks and make money. After that, companies would make their interest payments and then pay off the principal amount still due.
-- Reduce the value of the principal amount due for the licenses to reflect lower prices paid at earlier PCS auctions.
"This is an attempt to put things on the table," the FCC official said. "It's very unclear at this moment in what direction the commission is going."
The high prices paid for the licenses at last year's sale and the glut of new entrants into the wireless phone industry have made it tough for auction winners to raise financing.
Of the $10.2 billion bid at last year's PCS auction, the FCC had collected $973.3 million as of March.
In April, the FCC suspended the quarterly payments that were due while it mulled a request to annualize the payments. That move, according to one estimate, is costing Uncle Sam $1.5 million a day.
The FCC is asking the Treasury Department for help and advice.
